extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers and creative-writing students interested in narrative structure
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for selecting, experimenting with, and applying micro- and macro- narrative structures (vignettes, epistolary, in‑world artifacts, nonlinear timelines, etc.) to fiction projects. Emphasizes intentionality, reader expectations, and practical outlining techniques to discover appropriate structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explore alternative structures and avoid repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: There are nearly infinite structural options (stories told backwards; vignettes; letters; guidebooks; almanacs; etc.), so don’t get trapped into using the same structure again and again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try unfamiliar approaches to see what works for your story. Examples named: stories told backwards (Memento), books composed of vignettes (Invisible Cities). The goal is to play and expand your toolkit rather than defaulting to learned templates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of creator-facing vs consumer-facing aspects of structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The structures you use to create something are visible to you; the structures a reader perceives may be different (Howard’s music-notation analogy: creators see the double bar, readers hear the new key/note).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deploying a structure, consider both how it scaffolds your writing process and how it will be consumed. Design cues that translate the creator’s scaffolding into audible/visible signals for readers so they can follow transitions or movement in the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structures can complement — they are not exclusive
rubrics_metrics.description: Different structural techniques can coexist (a vignette collection can also follow three acts or Save the Cat, alternating perspectives, multiple timelines, or use footnotes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t feel forced to choose only one technique; combine complementary microstructures and macrostructures to serve the story. But be mindful of cognitive load; some combinations may 'break your brain' if overused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose structure based on what’s fun and exciting to you
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the measuring stick: 'does this sound like fun for me to do? Does this sound like fun for people to read?' — personal excitement and reader enjoyment are valid criteria for selecting a structural device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a structural choice doesn’t engage you as the creator, it will be hard to sustain. Practical note: monetary incentives can change willingness, but intrinsic excitement is the primary selection criterion discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use structure intentionally to highlight or diminish story aspects
rubrics_metrics.description: When you reframe a project with a different structure, ask: what aspects of the story does it heighten and what does it diminish? Not every structure will work for every story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Homework suggestion: reframe your current project or outline using a different structure, then analyze which elements are amplified (theme, character, setting, pacing) and which are reduced. Use that analysis to keep useful elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage audience expectations when using unfamiliar structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Introducing unfamiliar structures requires cues so the audience knows what to expect and doesn’t feel alienated (reference to reactions to Encanto’s unfamiliar structure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide signals or scaffolding early so readers can orient themselves. Think about how to prepare your audience for structural departures so novelty becomes engaging rather than disorienting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the '10‑year‑old boy excitedly tells you about his favorite movie' outlining technique to discover structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Outline or listen to an excited retelling of the story idea; repeated 'oh, oh, oh' moments highlight what the storyteller keeps returning to and can reveal necessary structural elements (alternate timelines, additional perspectives, artifacts, maps, countdowns).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This oral-tradition framing helps surface what the story wants to emphasize. Record or perform an excited retelling, note recurring hooks or elements, and let those guide whether you need multiple perspectives, timelines, or other structural devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate structure from form/genre and resist reductive mappings
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure (techniques like three-act, kishotentetsu, Save the Cat) is distinct from form/genre (cozy mystery, RPG rulebook, in-world artifact). Resist saying one structure is merely another under a different name (e.g., 'three act is just seven point without extra information').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat structures and forms as tools that help creators and consumers get from idea to finished story; map them thoughtfully rather than collapsing them into one another. Recognize when a structure is serving craft versus genre expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make artifacts and paratextual devices serve in-world logic and reader experience
rubrics_metrics.description: When creating in-world artifacts (e.g., a gamebook written as an in-world object, books with handwritten margin notes), choose such structures because they deepen the idea and are fun to make and read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether paratextual choices enhance the premise (Howard’s in-world RPG example: added 'artifactness' because it was fun and sold the concept). Ensure such devices don't exist solely for novelty — they should support storytelling and reader immersion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider vignette/fragment structures for different reader affect
rubrics_metrics.description: A vignette-based book (e.g., Invisible Cities) emphasizes places or moments over traditional plot: it allows pacing freedom, non-linear consumption, and an aggregate effect rather than a conventional arc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vignette structures when you want readers to sample, skip around, or experience an ensemble of moments rather than follow a single plotline. Be aware that this diminishes conventional plot-driven momentum and changes reader expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment intentionally (homework: reframe and evaluate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Actively reframe a project using structures discussed, especially ones you haven't tried, then evaluate the impact: what it heightens, what it diminishes, and which elements to keep.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a deliberate practice exercise: take an outline or draft, apply an alternate structure, and write/outline enough to see the effect. Use the results to decide whether to integrate elements going forward.
